title: Gauge and barrel length
summary: What 12 and 20 gauge mean, which chamber and barrel lengths shooters choose, and what the rules of Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting allow.

body.html: Gauge is counted the old way: the smaller the number, the wider the bore, so 12 gauge is wider than 20. FITASC allows guns no larger than 12 gauge, and most shooters use 12.

The number comes from an old measure: how many lead balls as wide as the bore together weigh one English pound (about 454 g). A 12-gauge bore is about 18.4–18.5 mm across, a 20-gauge bore about 15.6 mm.

Smaller gauges such as 20 or 28 are allowed in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting. The shot limit is the same for all guns: at most 28 g of lead shot (up to 2% more is tolerated). A 12 gauge carries this full load easily and gives a dense pattern.

A 20 gauge is lighter and often suits juniors and smaller shooters; youth models are often 20 gauge. It usually takes lighter cartridges, for example 21–24 g. But a light gun pushes harder into the shoulder, so a 20 gauge does not necessarily feel softer than a heavy 12 gauge.

The chamber length is marked on the barrel, most often 70 mm (2¾ in) or 76 mm (3 in); many modern competition guns have 76 mm chambers. Clay cartridges are usually 65–70 mm. The length on the box is the length of the case after firing, when its folded top (the crimp) has opened out. An unfired cartridge looks shorter than that number, so do not judge by eye: compare the number on the box with the chamber marking on the barrel. A shorter cartridge in a longer chamber is fine.
Never fire cartridges longer than the chamber marking. Check every time that the gauge on the cartridge matches the gauge of the gun.

Under the FITASC rules barrels must be at least 66 cm (26 in) long. In practice competition over-and-unders have 28 in (71 cm), 30 in (76 cm) or 32 in (81 cm) barrels. In Sporting™ many shooters choose 30 or 32 inches.

Longer barrels give a longer line for the eye and a smoother, steadier swing, but need a little more effort to get moving. Shorter ones are lighter and quicker, but easier to jerk. Barrel length changes the power of the shot very little; it mainly changes how the gun moves in your hands.
There is no single right length: it depends on your height, strength and style. A good way to choose is to try several guns with a coach.

notes.html: Gauge is not a measure in millimetres. Translate '12 gauge' as your language's '12 gauge', not as '12 mm'.

key_points.html: Gauge: smaller number, wider bore; FITASC maximum is 12 gauge.
FITASC: no larger than 12 gauge, barrels at least 66 cm (26 in) long.
The shot limit is the same for all gauges: at most 28 g of lead shot (up to 2% more is tolerated).
Do not fire cartridges longer than the chamber, and check that the gauge matches.
Many Sporting™ shooters use 30 or 32 inch barrels.

did_you_know.html: '12 gauge' means that 12 lead balls as wide as the bore weigh a pound together. Each ball would weigh about 38 g, more than the whole shot load allowed in a FITASC cartridge.

quiz.q: Which is the widest bore (largest gauge) the FITASC rules allow?
quiz.explain: The gauge may not be larger than 12; smaller gauges such as 20 are allowed. Remember: 10 gauge is wider than 12.

quiz.q: What is the minimum barrel length under the FITASC rules?
quiz.explain: Barrels must be at least 66 cm, that is 26 inches, in both disciplines.
The smaller the gauge number, the wider the bore: 12 gauge is about 18.4–18.5 mm, 20 gauge about 15.6 mm.
